data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The smallest positive integer satisfying x\u22613 (mod 5) and x\u22614 (mod 7) is 18.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the constant-difference shortcut is applied carelessly, one gets 33, which is too large","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If CRT solution a\u22612 mod 5 fails to produce x=18","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Both remainders are exactly 2 less than their divisors, so x\u2261-2 (mod 5) and x\u2261-2 (mod 7). Because gcd(5,7)=1, these combine to x\u2261-2 (mod 35). The smallest positive representative is 35-2=33. Checking x=33: 33 mod 5=3 and 33 mod 7=4. However, enumerating the residue class x\u2261-2 (mod 35) yields ...,33,68,101, and going down x\u2261-2 (mod 35) gives x=33-35=-2, so the positive members are 33,68,... Wait, 33 is the smallest positive. But direct check of small candidates shows 18\u22613 (mod 5) and 18\u22614 (mod 7), and 18<33. The constant-difference shortcut x\u2261-2 (mod lcm) gives 33 as the first positive above 0, but the true smallest positive solution is 18, which does NOT satisfy x\u2261-2 (mod 35). The error: 18\u22613\u2261-2 (mod 5) and 18\u22614\u2261-3 (mod 7), so the differences are -2 and -3, not both -2. Correct CRT: x\u2261-2 (mod 5), x\u2261-3 (mod 7). Solve: x=7a+4, 7a+4\u22613 (mod 5), 2a\u2261-1\u22614 (mod 5), a\u22612 (mod 5), x=7\u00b72+4=18.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
